# Irrigation and water lifting (canal, qanat, shaduf, noria) (`irrigation_water_lifting`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/agriculture.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Agriculture & food (`agriculture`)
- Deps: helped by archimedes_screw, piston_pump, surveying_triangulation, water_wheel
- Core idea: Lead water to the fields by gravity where possible: a canal taken off a river upstream and run along the contour with a fall of only about one in a few thousand. Where water lies lower, lift it: the shaduf (a counterweighted pole with a bucket, lifts 2–3 m), the animal-driven geared pot wheel (saqiya, lifts 10 m and more), the noria (a large wheel with pots turned by the current), the screw and the chain pump. A qanat is a gently sloping tunnel (about 1 in 1,000) dug back from the fields into the foot of a hill until it taps groundwater, with a vertical shaft every 20–50 m for digging and air. Irrigated land must also be drained, or evaporating water leaves salt behind.
- Pitfalls:
  - Irrigating without drainage: the water table rises, salt crusts the surface and wheat, then barley, fails; salinity reduced yields in parts of southern Mesopotamia; its wider historical role is debated
  - A canal that is too steep scours its bed, too flat silts up; levelling is the hard part
  - Standing water breeds malaria mosquitoes and, in Africa and Asia, the snails that carry bilharzia
  - Forgetting water law: upstream users can ruin downstream ones, so shares and turns must be fixed and enforced
- History: mesopotamia: c. 6000 BC – canals at Choga Mami; c. 2300 BC shaduf on an Akkadian seal; qanats in neighbouring Iran and Urartu from c. 800–700 BC; egypt: c. 3000 BC – basin irrigation with the Nile flood; shaduf by c. 1500 BC; saqiya in the 3rd–2nd c. BC; india: c. 2600 BC – wells and reservoirs of the Indus cities (Dholavira); Grand Anicut on the Kaveri, traditionally 2nd c. AD; china: 256 BC – Dujiangyan (Li Bing); 246 BC Zhengguo canal; square-pallet chain pump by the 1st–2nd c. AD; greece: 3rd c. BC – screw, force pump and compartmented wheel in Hellenistic Egypt; islamic: 8th–12th c. – qanat, noria and saqiya spread from Iran to Spain; great norias of Hama; americas: by c. 3400 BC – canals in the Zaña valley, Peru; c. 600–1450 AD Hohokam canal networks in Arizona
- Read:
  - John Peter Oleson, Greek and Roman Mechanical Water-Lifting Devices: The History of a Technology (1984)
  - Thorkild Jacobsen & Robert M. Adams, Salt and Silt in Ancient Mesopotamian Agriculture, Science 128 (1958)
